405769.description: Grizz was tagged by researchers from BioPixel Oceans Foundation.

405770.name: Hanna Marie
405770.description: Hanna Marie was tagged by researchers from BioPixel Oceans Foundation.

406534.name: Fitzy
406534.description: Shark Fitzy was the largest male shark tagged during an expedition by collaborating researchers on Norfolk Island. This big boy was feisty, just like the boat captain father-son combo Luke and Dean Fitzpatrick (aka Fitzy). The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

406535.name: Headstone
406535.description: Shark Headstone was tagged by researchers in Headstone Bay, on Norfolk Island. She was the first shark of the expedition to be fitted with a satellite tag, so she was named after the bay researchers were working in. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

406742.name: Miamiti
406742.description: Shark Maimiti was the largest female tagged on an expedition by collaborating scientists at Norfolk Island and the only shark to be caught twice. She was named after Maimiti Christian, a Polynesia princess and the wife of Fletcher Christian -the mutineer of the HMS Bounty. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

406789.name: David
406789.description: Shark David was the smallest male tagged on an expedition by collaborating scientists at Norfold Island. He is named after the trip coordinator Mark Scott’s young son. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

406793.name: Emma
406793.description: Shark Emma was the smallest female tagged on an expedition by collaborating scientists to Norfolk Island. She is named after the trip coordinator Mark Scott’s young daughter. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

406820.name: Amy
406820.description: Amy was tagged by researchers from BioPixel Oceans Foundation.

407072.name: Fletcher
407072.description: Shark Fletcher was named after Fletcher Christian, the mutineer of the HMS Bounty, and settler of nearby Pitcairn Island. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

412932.name: Tintoela
412932.description: Shark Tintoela was named for her sweet disposition, as Tintoela means sweetheart in the Norfolk Island language. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

413146.name: Koru
413146.description: Shark Koru had a curled lower caudal fin, so she was named after the spiral shape based on the appearance of a new unfurling silver fern frond, an important Māori symbol. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

422455.name: Katya
422455.description: Katya was tagged by researchers from BioPixel Oceans Foundation.

485395.name: Evelyn
485395.description: Evelyn is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Evelyn” is named after the granddaughter of Pat and P.J. Murray. Pat is the president of the Coastal Conservation Association and avid conservationist. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Evelyn will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

509160.name: Junonia
509160.description: Junonia is the first loggerhead sea turtle ever to be satellite-tagged after nesting on Sanibel Island. Researchers from the Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation tagged Junonia after she successfully laid a nest on Sanibel Island, Florida. She had been previously encountered on Sanibel in 2016, 2018, and 2019! Junonia will be part of a study to learn more about the post-nesting movements, migratory pathways, and foraging grounds of loggerhead sea turtles that nest on the gulf coast of Florida. Since Junonia was nesting during the 2018 red tide bloom, the data will also contribute to a research project investigating the long term impacts of red tide events on the health and reproductive success of nesting sea turtles (Funded by the Florida RESTORE Act Centers of Excellence). All research authorized by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

530006.name: Andromache
530006.description: Andromache was the first tagged during OCEARCH's Expedition Massachusetts 2020. She was named by our partner, luxury Swiss watchmaker Ulysse Nardin, after the Greek character Andromache, who is a symbol of maternity, strength and courage.

535571.name: Martha
535571.description: Martha is the 4th white shark tagged during OCEARCH Expedition Massachusetts 2020. She is named after the island of Martha's Vineyard.

535575.name: Beacon
535575.description: Beacon is the 3rd shark tagged on OCEARCH's Expedition Massachusetts 2020. Beacon's name was chosen by our partner SeaWorld and just like his name suggests, we expect he'll be a guiding symbol of hope for our oceans. SeaWorld has supported wildlife rescue, rehabilitation and conservation efforts, and vital ocean health initatives like OCEARCH for decades.

538048.name: Norfolk
538048.description: Shark Norfolk was named after the island where she was tagged. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

544541.name: Breton
544541.description: Breton is the first shark tagged during OCEARCH's Expedition Nova Scotia 2020 and is named for all of the wonderful people of Cape Breton where he was tagged. Breton is the 5th shark OCEARCH has tagged at Scatarie Island in two years of working in the area, providing evidence that the region could offer predictable access to white sharks. Breton's name was chosen by our partner SeaWorld, a leader in wildlife rescue, rehabilitation, and vital ocean health initatives like OCEARCH's.

550002.name: Gladee
550002.description: Gladee is the fifth animal sampled during the Expedition Nova Scotia. There is an epic legend of Gladee's Canteen, a famous restaurant run by Gladee and her sister, that is a special example of a co-operative and communal spirit on a very dynamic beach. It's a popular Nova Scotia story about a pioneer family who, against odds, brought revelations to the isolated coastal community. The story reminds us of our own collaborative team, and the dynamic life on the ship today.

550003.name: Hirtle
550003.description: Hirlte was the third white shark tagged during OCEARCH's Expedition Nova Scotia 2020 and was named after Hirtle's Beach near where he was tagged.

551127.name: Nukumi
551127.description: Nukumi, pronounced noo-goo-mee, is named after the legendary wise old grandmother figure of the Native American Mi'kmaq people, a culture that has deep roots in Canadian Maritime provinces (particularly Nova Scotia). With the new data we've collected, this matriarch will share her wisdom with us for years to come. She will continue to help balance fish stocks in the surrounding waters, and we look forward to learning more from this wise guardian of our ocean's eco-system.

552908.name: Mahone
552908.description: Mahone is largest male shark tagged by OCEARCH in Canadian waters. He was tagged during OCEARCH's Expedition Nova Scotia 2020 near Lunenburg, Nova Scotia. He is named after Mahone Bay.

552909.name: Rose
552909.description: Rose was tagged on OCEARCH's Expedition Nova Scotia 2020 and named after Rose Bay not far from where she was tagged. Rose's name was chosen by our partner SeaWorld who has supported wildlife rescue, rehabilitation, and vital ocean health initatives like OCEARCH for decades.

552910.name: Acadia
552910.description: Acadia was tagged during OCEARCH's Expedition Nova Scotia. Her name pays homage to the French colonial roots in the Canadian Maritimes.

553908.name: Edithe
553908.description: Edithe was the eighth and final shark tagged on OCEARCH’s expedition Nova Scotia 2020. Edithe was named by first year master’s student Joseph Fotso from the University of Windsor who was part of the expedition crew for the entire trip. Joseph chose to name Edithe after his mother.

553910.name: Monomoy
553910.description: Monomoy is the first juvenile ever tagged by OCEARCH in the Cape Cod area. He is named after Monomoy Island near where he was tagged. Monomoy's name was chosen by our partner SeaWorld who has supported wildlife resuce, rehabilitation, and vital ocean health initatives like OCEARCH's for decades.

630211.name: Sterling
630211.description: Sterling is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. “Sterling” is named after Sterling Mchorse, an avid outdoorsman. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Sterling will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

655054.name: Bubba-3
655054.description: Bubba-3 is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Bubba-3” is named by Carl and Von Young in honor of their mother, who nicknamed her sons Bubba Jr., Bubba Dwight, and Bubba Von. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Bubba-3 will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

655105.name: Kate
655105.description: This tiger shark was tagged by Dr. Adam Barnett's team at the Biopixel Oceans Foundation and is being tracked in cooperation with OCEARCH.

655106.name: Collette
655106.description: This tiger shark was tagged by Dr. Adam Barnett's team at the Biopixel Oceans Foundation and is being tracked in cooperation with OCEARCH.

655110.name: Bryce
655110.description: Bryce is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Bryce” is named after Bryce Tomaneng, an avid outdoorsman and aspiring marine biologist. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. 658080.description: Freidi was named by the Norfolk Island school on the 2021 Norfolk expedition, and is in the island’s traditional language. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around this unique island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia or New Zealand.

658443.name: Freya
658443.description: Freya is a sub-adult female white shark and her name was chosen by our partner Sea World. The name translates to "Noble Woman". Freya was named in homage to the noble women researchers on both Expedition Carolinas and on all past research expeditions who are working to uncover crucial shark insights related to their species' conservation.

662567.name: Geoff
662567.description:
Geoff was named by the Norfolk Island school on the 2021 Norfolk expedition. One of the primary school children chose to name a shark after her friend Geoff, one of the locals who frequents the coffee shop her mom owns. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around this unique island the sharks use. 662714.name: Charlotte

663081.name: Isla Belle
663081.description: Isla Belle is named after Luke Fitzpatrick’s young daughter, born just before the 2021 expedition. Tiger Shark “Fitzy” (also a 4.2 m female) was named after Luke and father Dean Fitzpatrick on the 2020 expedition, so we will see if these same sized sharks follow a similar route one year apart. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around this unique island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia or New Zealand.

663199.name: Buc-ee
663199.description: Buc-ee is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. Buc-ee the Shortfin Mako shark is named by Arch ‘Beaver’ and Joanie Aplin, the owners and founders of Buc-ee’s, after the iconic roadside destination in Texas. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Buc-ee will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663200.name: BobHayes
663200.description: Bob Hayes is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Bob Hayes” is named after Bob Hayes, an acclaimed champion for marine conservation. Hayes was the longtime General Counsel for the Coastal Conservation Association and American Sportfishing Association. He is a founder and past Chairman of the Center for Sportfishing Policy and was inducted into the IGFA Hall of Fame in 2019 for his contributions to marine conservation. Through his career and ongoing service, he has been a part of successful efforts to establish federal gamefish status for iconic species such as Atlantic billfish, red drum, and striped bass. He was instrumental in the inclusion of freedom-to-fish language in federal law and was a key leader in the recent passage of the Modern Fish Act. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Bob Hayes will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663201.name: Fast Ball
663201.description: Fast Ball is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. Fast Ball the Shortfin Mako shark is named by Bobby Patton. Mr Patton is an ardent supporter of wildlife conservation and a steward of the resource through his Commissioner role with the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. He also owns the Los Angles Dodgers, and Fast Ball gets his name in honor of the team. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Fast Ball will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663218.name: Slinger
663218.description: Slinger is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. This Mako shark is named Slinger, the nickname given to Sam L. Susser when he worked in NY at Salomon Brothers as an analyst from 1985-1988. Mr. Susser is a 5th generation resident of Corpus Christi who grew up wanting to be a marine biologist studying sharks. He still has his beloved collection of books on sharks and marine life from his childhood in his library. His heroes growing up were Jacque Cousteau and Jack Nicklaus. Mr. Susser’s scientific aptitude was mediocre (even on his best days) so he ended up studying finance and presently serves as the Chairman of Susser Bank and the Corpus Christi Athletic Club. The Susser family is a long time and proud supporter of Texas A&M – Corpus Christi. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Slinger will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663219.name: Laureen
663219.description: Laureen is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Laureen” is named by Mike Pedrotti for his wife, Laureen McCullough Pedrotti, who loves to scuba dive and spend time enjoying the beaches and waters of the Gulf of Mexico. Mike and Laureen have provided continued support for aspiring marine biology students and are strong supporters of marine and wildlife conservation. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Laureen will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663738.name: Nancy
663738.description: Nancy is a Shortfin Mako shark tagged during a research expedition by scientists with the Harte Research Institute’s Center for Sportfish Science and Conservation at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi. “Nancy” is named after Nancy Durham, an avid offshore angler (including the greatest rally towel team member), and advocate for conservation of marine wildlife. Mako sharks are one of the fastest swimming fish in the ocean and are known to make large-scale movements. Tracking sharks like Nancy will inform scientists about their migration patterns and habitat use in the Gulf of Mexico, helping to promote the conservation of these majestic apex predators.

663822.name: Jap
663822.description: Jap was the only male caught on the 2021 expedition to Norfolk Island. He was named in memory of one of the local beloved Norfolk Islanders who went by the nickname ‘Jap’. Jap enjoyed following the movements of the sharks tagged on the 2020 expedition, and his home sits just above the bay where these sharks are caught and tagged. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around this unique island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia or New Zealand.

711247.name: Scotty 2
711247.description: The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around the island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia, New Zealand, or further.

714085.name: Nehsi
714085.description: Nehsi was named by the Norfolk Island school on the 2021 Norfolk expedition, and is in the island’s traditional language. The tiger sharks around Norfolk Island were tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia and the USA, to understand what areas around this unique island the sharks use. This is part of a larger research program to determine if these sharks hang around the offshore islands where they are tagged, or if they travel over to Australia or New Zealand.

812695.name: Stann
812695.description: Stann is an adult male silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis) tagged off Lighthouse Reef, Belize, as part of a cooperative program between shark fishers, Georgia Aquarium, the Belize Fisheries Department, and Mote Marine Laboratory. This program employs fishers in order to substantially reduce shark catch and provides data required for shark management.

812696.name: El Tigre
812696.description: El Tigre is an adult male tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) tagged off Glover’s Reef, Belize, as part of a cooperative program between shark fishers, Georgia Aquarium, the Belize Fisheries Department, and Mote Marine Laboratory. This program employs fishers in order to substantially reduce shark catch and provides data required for shark management.

812697.name: Alan
812697.description: Alan is an adult male tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) tagged off Gladden Spit, Belize, as part of a cooperative program between shark fishers, Georgia Aquarium, the Belize Fisheries Department and Mote Marine Laboratory. This program employs fishers in order to substantially reduce shark catch and provides data required for shark management.

812698.name: Belekin
812698.description: Belekin is a juvenile male silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis) tagged off Lighthouse Reef, Belize, as part of a cooperative program between shark fishers, Georgia Aquarium, the Belize Fisheries Department, and Mote Marine Laboratory. This program employs fishers in order to substantially reduce shark catch and provides data required for shark management.

813615.name: Saki
813615.description: The name "Saki" was chosen by Peace Luthern College, a local high school in Cairns. Saki was chosen because the word for shark in local Torres Strait Creole translates to "Sak". Since this shark is a female, Australians tend to lenghten names as a term of endearment. This is a name that represents local culture, as there are a large number of Torres Strait Islander students at Peace Luthern College.

817675.name: Perla
817675.description: This tiger shark was tagged by a collaborative effort funded by NOAA and led by Conservación ConCiencia in partnership with Mote Marine Laboratory with the assistance from commercial fisherman Rodolfo Abrams, and Charter Captain Luis Burgos. Perla is named after the coastal community located in Old San Juan called La Perla, where just a few miles offshore this tiger shark was caught, tagged and released.

842511.name: Olympia
842511.description: Olympia was chosen by our partners at SeaWorld, who have supported wildlife rescue, rehabilitation, conservation efforts, and vital ocean health initiatives like OCEARCH for decades. She was named in support of the amazing athletes currently competing in the Olympic games. Just as the Olympics bring the world together on a global stage, we hope Olympia will bring global awareness of sharks and the OCEARCH Mission.

842512.name: Tuck
842512.description: Tuck was named for the people of Nantucket who have been so great to us throughout the years we’ve spent in this region. At just a few years older than Olympia, it will be exciting to see where Tuck takes us as he matures. He marks the 2nd animal on Expedition New England 2021, and the 72nd animal tagged for our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study.

843214.name: Santiago
843214.description:
Santiago weighs 140lbs and is likely around 3 years old. He marks the third white shark sampled during Expedition New England 2021 and was named by our longtime partners at Costa Sunglasses. Costa has helped protect our waters for more than a decade with an OCEARCH collection that supports our work and spreads the message “Don’t Fear The Fin”.


The "Santiago" model of sunglasses is part of Costa’s “Untangle Our Oceans” initiative made from recycled fishing nets to ensure a future full of fish - and sharks - for generations to come. We are excited to amplify the importance of keeping our oceans free of plastic.

847691.name: Lil' Smack
847691.description: Lil’ Smack is a great hammerhead tagged by the Marine Fisheries Ecology Program at Mississippi State University. This shark was named after Lil’ Smack IPA, a craft beer brewed in Gulfport, MS, by Chandeleur Island Brewing Company. Chandeleur Island Brewing Company is committed to supporting projects that help conserve and protect iconic species like the great hammerhead. Globally, great hammerheads are considered Critically Endangered, and their population status in the United States is currently unknown. Tracking sharks like Lil’ Smack will provide much-needed information about great hammerhead movements, migrations, and habitat use.

858430.name: Scot
858430.description:
Scot is an adult white shark sampled off West Ironbound Island. Scot marks the 74th white shark tagged, sampled, and released by OCEARCH in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean, and the first white shark sampled during Expedition Nova Scotia 2021. 


He was named by our partners at SeaWorld, who have supported wildlife rescue rehabilitation and conservation efforts, and vital ocean health initiatives like OCEARCH for decades. He was named Scot after the people of Nova Scotia, who have always been so welcoming and committed to the science and health of our oceans.  Thanks to everyone on the team that helped us get to number 74 in our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study and have allowed us to continue our work on our sharks and our oceans!

859287.name: Sable
859287.description:
Sable marks the 76th shark sampled, tagged, and released in our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study and the third of Expedition Nova Scotia 2021.


She was named Sable after the Sable Island National Park Reserve, located approximately 180 miles offshore of Halifax, Nova Scotia, near where she was tagged. Sable Island National Park Reserve is known for its immense wildlife, including the world’s largest breeding colony of grey seals, wild horses, and a variety of plants and insects that are found nowhere else on earth.

865112.name: Hali
865112.description:
Hali marks the 2nd shark sampled, tagged, and released on Expedition Nova Scotia 2021, and our 75th shark in our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study. 


She was named Hali for the people of Halifax, Nova Scotia who have been so wonderful to us every time we visit this region. Their commitment to science with an ocean first disposition has made this area a true joy to work in. Hali was named by our partners at SeaWorld, who have supported wildlife rescue rehabilitation and conservation efforts, and vital ocean health initiatives like OCEARCH for decades.

865246.name: Sarah
865246.description:
Sarah marks the 4th white shark sampled, tagged, and released during Expedition Nova Scotia 2021 and the 77th shark of our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study!


Sarah was named after Sarah Fischer, OCEARCH Founder and Expedition Leader Chris Fischer's daughter. Sarah Fischer was able to join the OCEARCH crew during a previous expedition to assist our science team with sample collection and learn more about OCEARCH's work on our sharks and our oceans. We are excited to see where Sarah the shark takes us as she continues to grow into adulthood and what Scientist in Training Sarah Fischer will help us learn in the future!

865303.name: Ulysses
865303.description:
Ulysses is the 6th white shark sampled, tagged, and released during Expedition Nova Scotia 2021 and the 79th shark of our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study. He was the third shark sampled on September 14th, 2021!


He is boldly named after the founder of OCEARCH partner and fine Swiss watch manufacturer Ulysse Nardin. Ulysses, the true definition of exploration and bravery, is not only a tribute to the great Swiss watchmaker but also the Roman name for Odysseus, the Greek hero of the Iliad. Heralded by Homer, lauded by Tennyson and Joyce, Ulysses has been used to name ships, submarines, spacecraft, and now a magnificent Great White Shark. May he long explore our seas!

865390.name: Maple
865390.description:
Maple is a sub-adult female, our 2nd shark sampled, tagged, and released on September 14th.  Maple was named after the maple leaf, one of Canada’s national emblems.


It has been such a pleasure working in Atlantic Canada over the past four years and we hope that Maple helps honor our gratitude for this region and its people for years to come. She had a distinctive wound on the left side of her body and after the initial assessment, our science team believes it was likely due to a recent interaction with another larger white shark. This interaction was possibly an example of dominance behavior. It is not uncommon for sharks to show their dominance over a smaller animal of their species by delivering a significant but non-fatal bite.

866912.name: Sail
866912.description: Sail is a great hammerhead tagged by the Marine Fisheries Ecology Program at Mississippi State University. Sail is named in honor of Mississippi Aquarium’s iconic sails which stand over 60 feet tall and overlook the Gulf of Mexico. The sails symbolize education, conservation, and community. Since its opening on August 29, 2020, the Aquarium has propelled forward to serve the community and ocean environments by creating and supporting new experiences through quality education and research. Globally, great hammerheads are considered Critically Endangered, and their population status in the United States is currently unknown. Tracking sharks like Sail will provide much-needed information about great hammerhead movements, migrations, and habitat use.

867210.name: Bob
867210.description: Bob is named after our former chief scientist Dr. Robert (Bob) Hueter who has been a pioneer in shark science for over 40 years. His research has produced over 200 published papers and he has made a profound impact on the conservation and management of sharks globally. Bob continues to help OCEARCH push science further by bringing together a team of multi-disciplinary scientists to collaborate on over 24 research projects designed to unravel the mysteries of the white shark in the North Atlantic Ocean. We’ll be following the journeys of both Bob the shark and Dr. Bob Hueter as they continue to help us grow in the world of science for the betterment of our sharks and our oceans.

867480.name: Tancook
867480.description:
Tancook means "facing the open sea" to the local indigenous Mi'kmaq people of Nova Scotia. We met Tancook off West Ironbound Island, which is just south of Tancook Island, a place that was once a summer fishing ground for the indigenous people.


Tancook marks the 81st shark of our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study and our 8th of Expedition Nova Scotia 2021. We’re looking forward to Tancook teaching us more about the open sea as we follow along with his movements!

867481.name: Keji
867481.description:
Keji is named after the Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site, which is located in the region near where we were able to sample, tag, and release him. The Kejimkujik National Park is a cultural landscape that was first inhabited by the indigenous Mi’kmaq people. The abundance of petroglyphs and historic travel routes hold the memories and stories of the people in this region long ago.


He marks the 9th shark sampled, tagged, and released on Expedition Nova Scotia 2021 and our 82nd shark of our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study.

867785.name: Flower
867785.description:
Flower marks our 10th shark sampled, tagged, and released on Expedition Nova Scotia 2021, and our 83rd of our Northwest Atlantic White Shark Study.


Flower is named after our friends the Flower family who have been incredible to us throughout our years in Nova Scotia. Since helping us become familiar with the area during our first visit to Nova Scotia in 2018 to their continued support over the past four years, we are extremely grateful for the entire Flower family.

885626.name: Pete
885626.description:
Pete was tagged by our collaborators at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation to better understand the habitat use of Tiger Sharks off Queensland, Australia.


Pete is a tiger shark tagged at Lady Elliot eco-resort. He is named after the resort owner Peter Gash who is a pioneer of ecotourism on the Great Barrier Reef.

885628.name: Zozo
885628.description:
Zozo was tagged by our collaborators at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation to better understand the habitat use of Tiger Sharks off Queensland, Australia.

Zozo is named after Adam Barnett's daughter, Zoe. Adam is a research fellow with James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation.

885795.name: Z-River
885795.description:
Z-River was tagged by our collaborators at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation to better understand the habitat use of Tiger Sharks off Queensland, Australia. Z-River is the largest male tiger shark satellite tagged on the Great Barrier Reef, and named after Adam Barnett's son, Zake.

Adam Barnett is a research fellow with James Cook University and Biopixel Ocean Foundation.

894870.name: Chloe
894870.description:
Chloe was sampled by our collaborators at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation to better understand the habitat use of Tiger Sharks off Queensland, Australia.

Chloe was tagged at Lady Elliot Island with support from the island eco-resort. The shark is named after Chloe Gash the younger daughter of the resort owner.

985813.name: Ali
985813.description: Ali is a whale shark tagged by our colleagues at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation. The expedition was funded by BLANCPAIN. Ali is named after Alison Huveneers, a guest we had on the trip (helping her husband's research) and it was her birthday the day we tagged this shark!

985814.name: Blancpain
985814.description: This whale shark was tagged by our colleagues at James Cook University and Biopixel Oceans Foundation. The expedition was funded by BLANCPAIN, and thus how this shark received its name!

985851.name: Fifty Fathoms
985851.description: This whale shark was tagged by colleagues at James Cook University and researchers from Biopixel Oceans Foundation. The expedition was funded by BLANCPAIN, and Fifty Fathoms is their dive watch.

987168.name: Alexios
987168.description: Alexois is a whale shark tagged by our colleagues at James Cook University and Biopoxel Oceans Foundation. The expedition was funded by BLANCPAIN. Alexois is the contact our colleague's laisse with at BLNCPAIN!

1100935.name: Kimmy
1100935.description:
Kimmy is named after a team member's partner, Kimberley Batley, currently doing a post-doc in Sydney, Australia. 


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

1100943.name: Tinka
1100943.description:
Tinka is named after a Norfolk Island local dog that kept the research team company during morning coffee runs.


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

Rocket was named by two Norfolk Island kids who came to listen to the research team giving a presentation to the local community.


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

Lacky is named after the lactate analysis that we take to assess post-capture stress of tiger sharks.


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

1101254.description:

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

1101543.name: Theodosia

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island

Tigger was named by a local Norfolk Island resident who came to listen to the research team giving a presentation to the local community.


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

1106959.name: Ali-Bel
1106959.description:
Ali-Bel is named after team members' wifes, Alison Huveneers and Annabel Smith, who have put up with their partners being frequently away in the field to tag sharks.


This shark was tagged by an international team of scientists from Australia (Flinders University, James Cook University) and the USA (Georgia Aquarium) to understand the movements, diet, and microbiome of tiger sharks around Norfolk Island.

1167289.name: Crystal
1167289.description:
We met this beautiful female, juvenile white shark on Monday, March 14th while drifting off of North Carolina. She hung out with us for a while, circling the ship a few times, before we were able to study her on the lift. We collected samples for 25 different science projects including blood and muscle samples, as well as the attachment of a SPOT tag and a biologger package that was deployed for 16 hours. 


Crystal was named after North Carolina’s Crystal Coast, a stretch of beaches located near where we were able to sample and tag her and is known as the Southern Outer Banks. Crystal is our first and only white shark studied during Expedition Carolinas 2022 and our 84th shark sampled and tagged in our Western North Atlantic White Shark Study.

1479798.name: Simon
1479798.description: Simon marks the 86th white shark sampled, tagged and released in our Western North Atlantic White Shark study and our 2nd during Expedition Southbound. He is named after St. Simons Island, an island in Georgia, near where we met him.

1480119.name: Ormond

1480814.name: Jekyll
1480814.description: Jekyll is our 87th white shark tagged in the Western North Atlantic and our 3rd during Expedition Southbound! He was named by OCEARCH’s community in honor of Jekyll Island, Georgia near where we met him.

1483470.name: Frosty
1483470.description: Frosty is our 88th shark sampled, tagged and released in the Western North Atlantic and our 4th during Expedition Southbound 2022. We embarked on Expedition Southbound to learn more about these animals as they begin their winter residency and we named this shark Frosty to celebrate this winter season.

1561596.name: Anne Bonny
1561596.description: Anne Bonny is our 90th white shark tagged in the Western North Atlantic and our 2nd during Expedition Northbound.  She was named after the notorious female pirate that frequented the waters around Cape Hatteras in the early 1700s, near where she was tagged.  Anne Bonny was a pioneer of her time and we’re excited to see what Anne Bonny the shark will teach our scientists.

1561597.name: Ocracoke
1561597.description: Ocracoke is our 91st white shark tagged in the Western North Atlantic and our 3rd during Expedition Northbound.  We named this male shark Ocracoke after Ocracoke Island which is located close to where we met him.

1561937.name: Penny
1561937.description: Penny is our 92nd white shark tagged in the Western North Atlantic and our 4th during Expedition Northbound.  She is named after our friends at Salty Penny Canvas in Morehead City, NC. They have helped our team with custom marine canvas projects that provide a more comfortable experience on the water and allow us to operate in tougher conditions. We’re grateful for the Penny family for their support of our research and can’t wait to see what Penny the shark teaches us.

2015262.name: B.P. Armstrong
2015262.description:
The conservation programs of Cooperativa Turística Kab Xok and Saving Our Sharks have now partnered with Ch’ooj Ajauil AC in monitoring sharks off the northeast Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico.  This male great hammerhead shark was named Bob Patricio Armstrong by shark 'adopter' Rebecca Armstrong who kindly donated the satellite tag.


 


Kab Xok (‘shark world’ in Mayan), is a Cooperative formed by fishermen from Isla Mujeres dedicated to the monitoring and conservation of sharks and marine life through nature tourism and citizen science.


Saving Our Sharks is a non-profit organization that has been dedicated to the conservation and research of sharks and marine life in the Mexican Caribbean for more than 13 years.


Ch'ooj Ajauil (meaning ‘blue lordship’ in Mayan), is a non-profit organization devoted to ensuring a healthy and sustainable future for the marine biodiversity of Mexican waters.

2106508.name: Buffett
2106508.description:
On the evening of June 29 (and morning of June 30), 2023 Caretta Research Project Biologists and Dan Evans, a collaborator from the Sea Turtle Conservancy, attached satellite transmitters to two adult loggerheads with the goal of tracking their moments after nesting on Wassaw, GA. Dr. Brian Shamblin, collaborator and geneticist with UGA, has helped us locate past and present relatives of our satellite tagged females to learn more about how their lineage plays a role in nesting and conservation. Through the genetic research, Dr. Brian Shamblin has established that Buffett has one half sister in the Northern Recovery Unit who nested on Ossabaw Island, GA twice in 2022. Buffet first nested on Wassaw in 2016, and has since produced 11 nests on Wassaw, returning in 2020 and 2023.


Buffett was named in honor of the late Jimmy Buffett, American singer and songwriter. Jimmy Buffett was an advocate and supporter of conservation efforts for sea life, including manatees and sea turtles.

2106696.name: Caroline (Sea Turtle)
2106696.description:
On June 29 of 2023 Caretta Research Project Biologists and Dan Evans, a collaborator from the Sea Turtle Conservancy, attached satellite transmitters to two adult loggerheads with the goal of tracking their moments after nesting on Wassaw. Dr. Brian Shamblin, collaborator and geneticist with UGA, has helped locate past and present relatives of the satellite tagged females to learn more about how their lineage plays a role in nesting and conservation. Through genetic research, Dr. Brian Shamblin has established that Caroline has two full sisters and one half sister in the Northern Recovery Unit who nested on the GA and FL coasts in 2019 and 2020. She also has a Wassaw Mom, who was first tagged in 1996 and was last seen on Wassaw in 2022. Caroline first nested on Wassaw in 2020, and has since laid 7 nests on the island, returning in 2023.


Caroline is named after Caroline Gable, President and CEO at The Shared Earth Foundation, a long-time supporter of CRP. This Satellite tag was sponsored by Barbara and Larry Perlis to honor all that Caroline has done for the loggerhead sea turtle population through our conservation efforts.

2107356.name: Windy
2107356.description: Windy was first seen on Juno Beach, Florida in 2003 and has since been encountered nesting 9 times by researchers at Loggerhead Marinelife Center. Tagging partners include Loggerhead Marinelife Center and Florida Atlantic University Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

2108458.name: Bootes
2108458.description: Bootes was first seen on Juno Beach, Florida in 2002. She is one of the first leatherbacks tagged under the Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s leatherback tagging program, which has identified and tagged over 700 leatherback sea turtles on Juno Beach since its inception in 2001, with the goals of analyzing migration patterns, clutch frequency (i.e., how many nests does one turtle lay in a single nesting season?), health, toxicology, injury and disease prevalence, nest temperatures, and other human-related impacts on the local nesting aggregation. Bootes is named after the Boötes constellation and has been seen 17 times since her initial encounter. Funding for the satellite tag was provided by a grant awarded from the Sea Turtle Grants Program. The Sea Turtle Grants Program is funded from proceeds from the sale of the Florida Sea Turtle License Plates. Learn more at www.helpingseaturtles.org.

2108767.name: Patricia
2108767.description: Patricia was first seen on Juno Beach, Florida in 2005. She has been encountered three times since the initial encounter, and is the heaviest turtle weighed by researchers for Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s on-going leatherback body condition study. Tagging partners include the Loggerhead Marinelife Center and the Florida Atlantic University Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

2108876.name: Eleanor
2108876.description: Researchers from Loggerhead Marnelife Center tagged Eleanor after she laid her first nest of the 2024 nesting season on Juno Beach, Florida. Eleanor was named after Eleanor Fletcher, the long-time Juno Beach resident that founded what is now Loggerhead Marinelife Center. Eleanor is a part of a long-term study aimed at understanding loggerhead clutch frequency, or the number of nests a single female lays within one breeding season. This project was funded in part by a grant awarded from the Sea Turtle Grants Program. The Sea turtle Grants Program is funded from proceeds from the sale of the Florida Sea Turtle License Plate. Learn more at helpingseaturtles.org.

Learn more at helpingseaturtles.org. This terrfic photo of Lemon Drop comes courtesy of scuba diver Matthew Reyer who spotted her resting on a reef off Boca Raton, FL (June 18, 2024). Thank you Matthew!

2108894.name: Dolly2
2108894.species: Loggerhead x Hawksbill Hybrid (Caretta caretta x Eretmochelys imbricata)
2108894.description: Researchers from Loggerhead Marnelife Center tagged Dolly after she laid her first nest of the 2024 nesting season on Juno Beach, Florida. Dolly, named after Dolly Parton,  is a unique turtle that displayed features of both loggerhead and hawksbill sea turtles and had our researchers scratching their heads. Genetic analysis revealed that Dolly is a hybrid turtle that is half loggerhead and half hawksbill!

2139731.name: Urdintxo
2139731.description:
During Expedition Save the Med, blue shark Urdintxo was tagged by Spanish researchers in the Bay of Biscay, in Lastres Canyon, North of Spain. “Urdintxo” means “little blue” in the local Basque language, the oldest spoken language known in Europe. The project aims to understand the habitat use and migration patterns of pelagic sharks in the Bay of Biscay, as well as the area's importance to those species (reproduction, feeding, nursery area). The Basque Government has funded the project through European resources to support the EU Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), the EU Maritime Policy and the EU agenda for international ocean governance.


Spanish


“Urdintxo” fue marcado por personal investigador español en el Cañón de Lastres, golfo de Vizcaya, al norte de España durante la primera expedición salvar al Mediterráneo. “Urdintxo” significa pequeño azul en Euskera, la lengua hablada más antigua conocida en Europa. El proyecto tiene como objetivo entender el uso del hábitat y los patrones de migración de los tiburones pelágicos n el golfo de Vizcaya, así como la importancia del área para estas especies (reproducción, alimentación, zona de crianza). El Gobierno Vasco ha financiado este proyecto a través de los fondos europeos que tiene como fin respaldar la política pesquera común de la UE (PPC), la política marítima de la UE y la agenda de la UE para la gobernanza internacional de los océanos.


Basque


“Urdintxo”, Mediterraneoa salbatzeko lehen espedizioan markatua izan zen ikerlari espainiarrengatik Lastresko arroilan, Bizkaiko Golkoan, Espainia iparraldean. “Urdintxo” jarri zaio marrazo urdin honi, bere koloreagatik.  Proiektuak Bizkaiko Golkoan marrazo pelagikoen habitataren erabilera eta migrazio-patroiak ulertzea du helburu, baita eremu honek espezie horientzat duen garrantzia ere (ugalketa, elikadura, haztegi-eremu bezala). Eusko Jaurlaritzak Europako diru-laguntzen bidez finantzatu du proiektu hau, zeinak Europar Batasuneko arrantza politika komunari (CFP), EBko itsas politikari eta EBko nazioarteko ozeanoen gobernantzarako agendari laguntzea duen helburu.

2141156.name: Félix
2141156.description:
The conservation programs of Cooperativa Turística Kab Xok and Saving Our Sharks have now partnered with Ch’ooj Ajauil AC in monitoring sharks off the northeast Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico.  This male great hammerhead shark was named Félix by the García family who 'adopted' this shark and kindly donated the satellite tag.  


Kab Xok (‘shark world’ in Mayan), is a Cooperative formed by fishermen from Isla Mujeres dedicated to the monitoring and conservation of sharks and marine life through nature tourism and citizen science.


Saving Our Sharks is a non-profit organization that has been dedicated to the conservation and research of sharks and marine life in the Mexican Caribbean for more than 13 years.


Ch'ooj Ajauil (meaning ‘blue lordship’ in Mayan), is a non-profit organization devoted to ensuring a healthy and sustainable future for the marine biodiversity of Mexican waters.

2344827.name: Kando
2344827.description: Meet Kando, the Tiger Shark Kando, a majestic tiger shark, was tagged on January 13, 2025, as part of OCEARCH’s ongoing research off the FL/GA coast, about 45 miles offshore. This adult female shark weighs an estimated 405 lbs and measures 10 feet in length, making her a stunning example of her species. Named "Kando," a Japanese word describing the simultaneous feelings of deep satisfaction and excitement from encountering something truly exceptional, her name reflects the profound impact the ocean and its creatures have on us. Kando embodies the awe and inspiration we feel for marine life, perfectly aligning with our mission to protect and understand these magnificent animals. Kando is named in honor of Yamaha, a long-time partner whose support has been crucial in advancing our research. We’re thrilled to follow her journey as we continue to unravel the mysteries of the ocean.

2344838.name: Danny
2344838.description:
Danny, a male white shark, was tagged off the coast near the Florida/Georgia line on January 17, 2025. At 9.5 feet in length and weighing an estimated 462 lbs, Danny is currently a subadult, part of the Western North Atlantic white shark population. This shark is outfitted with both a SPOT and PSAT tag, enabling us to track his movements and collect real-time data for approximately 5 years.


Danny’s journey is particularly special as he’s named after one of OCEARCH’s biggest fans and supporters. His story continues the legacy of global community collaboration in ocean conservation. By tracking Danny, we’re not only unlocking new insights into the life history of white sharks but also connecting to the people like Danny who help make this research possible. We’ll continue to follow his travels and look forward to uncovering more about his role in the ecosystem as well as his migration patterns. Through ongoing efforts like these, we aim to deepen our understanding of sharks and continue our work toward protecting these incredible creatures. Stay tuned for more updates on Danny’s journey and his important role in ocean conservation!

2344847.name: Contender
2344847.description: Meet Contender, the ultimate ocean warrior! This powerful white shark was tagged on January 17, 2025, off the FL/GA coast, about 45 miles offshore. At 13.8 feet long and weighing an estimated 1,653 lbs, Contender is a mature male now contributing to OCEARCH’s mission of shark research and ocean conservation. The SPOT tag deployed on Contender will provide valuable real-time data for approximately five years, helping us track his movements and understand his migration patterns. Additionally, we've collected important biological samples, including urogenital material, which are currently being analyzed. Contender’s name is in honor of Contender Boats, a longtime OCEARCH partner, whose industry-leading sport fishing and pleasure boats enable our research missions. Their commitment to performance and innovation is essential to our ability to explore and protect our oceans. Stay tuned as we continue following Contender on his journey to help protect sharks and the ocean ecosystem!

2361676.name: Dold
2361676.description: A White Shark Tagged on National Science Day! Meet Dold, a 761-lb, 11 ft. 2 in. subadult male white shark, now part of the OCEARCH Western North Atlantic White Shark Study. Tagged 45 miles offshore near the FL/GA line, Dold will provide critical data on the movements and behaviors of this essential apex predator. Dold is named in honor of Dr. Christopher Dold of SeaWorld, a key figure in ocean conservation. Dr. Dold influenced the OCEARCH collaborative science model, helping connect experts together to drive shark research forward. Under his leadership, SeaWorld has been instrumental in marine animal rescue, rehabilitation, and conservation, aiding tens of thousands of animals in need. By tracking Dold, we’ll gain deeper insights into white shark migration, health, and their role in maintaining ocean balance. Learn more about the SeaWorld Conservation Fund and their impact: https://swbg-conservationfund.org/ Tap the heart to follow Dold’s journey on the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker!

2431093.name: Morada
2431093.description:
We’re thrilled to introduce Morada, an adult female tiger shark who now joins the OCEARCH Global Shark tracker, helping us better understand this shark species that lives in the western North Atlantic.


Tagged and sampled 5 nautical miles offshore of Islamorada, Florida, with collaborators from Ocean First Institute and Key Dives, she measured 11 feet, 2 inches and weighs an estimated 761 Ibs. During the tagging process, OCEARCH Chief Scientist and Veterinarian Dr. Harley Newton conducted an onboard ultrasound, confirming that Morada is pregnant and carrying the next generation of apex predators!


She was named in honor of Islamorada Island, the “Purple Island,” named by early Spanish explorers inspired by the island’s vibrant sunsets and blooming purple bougainvillea. Just like her namesake, Morada represents natural beauty, strength, and the deep connection between our environment and the creatures that call it home.


‘Momma Morada’ is a powerful example of the vital role apex predators play in balancing marine ecosystems. Tiger sharks maintain marine ecosystem balance by regulating prey populations, influencing the behavior of other species to prevent overgrazing of critical habitats like seagrass beds and coral reefs, and promoting healthy, resilient marine life through natural selection by preying on the sick, injured, or weak.


Let Morada serve as a reminder: there is beauty all around us — in nature, in science, and in the mission to protect both. Follow Morada’s journey in the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker — and be part of the story.

2431784.name: Hanna

2548468.name: Mira
2548468.description:
Meet Mira, a Newly Tagged Dusky Shark!


On May 15, 2025, the OCEARCH team tagged and sampled Mira, an adult female dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) off the coast of Jacksonville, Florida. Mira is OCEARCH’s first Dusky shark tagged, sampled, and released.  She measured 9 feet, 8 inches and weighed an estimated 327 lbs, Mira is just above the known size for maturity in this species.


Dusky sharks are globally endangered and considered vulnerable in the North Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. Like white sharks, they have small litters, late maturity, and a three-year reproductive cycle—including nearly two years of gestation followed by a year of rest. Mira did not show signs of pregnancy or recent mating, offering a valuable data point on her life stage.


Named Mira, which means “wonder” and is also a star in the night sky, this shark reminds us how much there is still to learn about this species. Track Mira’s journey for free and follow our work to better understand and protect dusky sharks.

2789925.name: Jason
2789925.description:
Meet Jason, the first white shark tagged and released by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams.


Jason was tagged in Mahone Bay on July 16, 2025, as part of a collaboration between Dr. Nigel Hussey of the University of Windsor and OCEARCH to study white sharks during their summer/fall residency period in Atlantic Canada. Jason is a subadult male, measuring 9 feet 4 inches in total length and estimated to weigh 510 lbs. Atlantic Canada and Newfoundland are important parts of the white shark’s range, making them essential areas for managing the western North Atlantic population. Additional tagging efforts—including satellite-linked and acoustic tags—will aid scientists and policymakers in understanding white shark abundance in the region, their distribution and critical habitats, and how their presence has changed over time.


Inspired by his experience as a master’s student at the Bimini Biological Field Station in the Bahamas, it has long been Dr. Hussey’s dream to create a similar “living marine lab” for students and researchers in Nova Scotia, Canada. After witnessing the number of white sharks tagged and released during the first OCEARCH expedition to Atlantic Canada in 2018, Dr. Hussey worked to establish a community-based field station on Big Tancook Island in Mahone Bay. Jason is the first white shark to be tagged from this new field station.


Jason is named in honor of a longtime friend of Dr. Hussey’s, Jason Carter, who recently passed after a long battle with cancer. Jason was instrumental in the journey to establish the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station, and his attitude toward hard work and facing challenges head-on epitomizes the vision of the station. We’re thrilled to follow his journey as we continue to reveal the importance of Atlantic Canada to the western North Atlantic white shark.

2790721.name: Bella
2790721.description:
Meet Bella, a newly tagged white shark helping to shape the future of ocean conservation.


On July 18th, 2025, Bella was tagged and released in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams and Dr. Nigel Hussey of the University of Windsor. This effort is part of a larger research initiative to better understand the movements, behaviors, and life history of white sharks during their seasonal presence in Atlantic Canada—a vital region for the conservation of the species in the western North Atlantic.


At the time of tagging, Bella was a large juvenile female, measuring 10 feet 2 inches and weighing approximately 729 lbs. Her presence in these waters adds valuable data to the growing body of research about how white sharks use Canadian coastal habitats during the summer and fall months.


Bella’s name, meaning “beautiful” in Italian, holds special significance. She was named in honor of one of OCEARCH’s biggest fans and supporters in Florida, representing the passionate global community that fuels this important work. Her story is a testament to the power of collaboration—from world-class scientists and fishermen to everyday ocean lovers.


By tracking Bella’s movements, researchers will gain insights into migration patterns, habitat use, and the role of Canadian waters in the life cycle of white sharks. But her journey is more than just scientific; it’s a symbol of the collective effort it takes to protect them.


Bella’s tagging continues the legacy of OCEARCH’s mission to advance ocean science while engaging the public in real-time, open-access research. We invite you to follow her journey and be a part of this shared commitment to preserving the ocean for generations to come.

2790722.name: Baker
2790722.description:
Meet Baker, a newly tagged adult white shark whose story is deeply connected to the heart of the community that made his tagging possible.


On July 21st, 2025, Baker was tagged and released in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams and Dr. Nigel Hussey of the University of Windsor. This effort is part of an ongoing initiative to study white sharks during their summer and fall residency in Atlantic Canada—a key region for the species in the western North Atlantic.


Baker is an adult male white shark, measuring an impressive 12 feet 10 inches in length and weighing approximately 1,429 lbs. His presence in Canadian waters provides invaluable data on the migratory behaviors, habitat preferences, and overall ecology of mature white sharks—an age group that remains less understood compared to juveniles.


He was named in honor of David Baker, a dedicated community member whose hard work, vision, and support were central to launching the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station. David’s contributions have helped shape the station into a hub for collaborative, community-rooted marine research.


Tracking Baker is more than just monitoring a shark; it’s about following a symbol of what can be accomplished when science, community, and conservation come together. His journey embodies the spirit of connection between people and the ocean—and how local action can have global impact.


As Baker roams the North Atlantic, he will continue to teach us more about this iconic species while honoring the individuals who make this work possible. Follow Baker’s path as we work together to understand and protect the white shark and the ecosystems they call home.

2794989.name: Quint

2803818.name: Percy
2803818.description:
Meet Percy, Percy was tagged and sampled on July 28th, 2025, Percy was tagged and released in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams. Percy is a 9-foot, 9-inch sub-adult male white shark, weighing an estimated 432 pounds at the time of tagging.


Percy is the sixth shark tagged during our summer residency field research study and carries a name that honors new beginnings—he was named after the newest resident of the Tancook Islands, born on July 21st, and the eighth generation of the Cross Family to call the island home. Just like his namesake, Percy represents a connection to both legacy and the future—linking local community heritage with global ocean conservation.


As Percy begins his journey through the western North Atlantic, we look forward to learning more from him and sharing his story with the world. Track Percy now on the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker app.

2812382.name: Cayo
2812382.description: Meet Cayo, a newly tagged white shark on July 29th, 2025, Cayo was tagged and released in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams. At the time of tagging, Cayo measured 10 feet 3 inches and is classified as a large juvenile female white shark. Cayo was named in honor of YETI, a generous and long-time partner of OCEARCH whose support has been vital to advancing our mission. The name “Cayo” nods to the brand’s roots in the coastal and fishing communities, where conservation and adventure go hand in hand. As Cayo begins her journey through the western North Atlantic, she carries with her a legacy of partnership, purpose, and discovery. Track her movements now on the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker app and follow her migration patterns.

2812557.name: Wassaw Will

2812565.name: Lillian-Hazel
2812565.description:
This turtle was tagged by the Archie Carr Center for Sea Turtle Research in partnership with the Caretta Research Project. Her name was given by the “Adopt a Turtle” initiative and Littlewood Elementary School.


Lillian Hazel was first tagged in 2008 on Wassaw NWR. We don’t know where she went for 6 years, but she returned to nest in 2015, 2017, 2020, and 2025. In 2022 she also nested 4 times on St. Catherine’s Island, but overall has laid 21 nests on Wassaw NWR.  She has a documented grand total of 2,424 eggs, and 1,256 hatchlings that emerged. At least 6 documented nests have been lost to storms or tidal surge. Through the genetics project run by Dr. Brain Shamblin at UGA, we have determined that Lillian does not have any known relatives in the North Atlantic Recovery Unit at this time.

2812567.name: Kegan-Magnolia
2812567.description:
This turtle was tagged by the Archie Carr Center for Sea Turtle Research in partnership with the Caretta Research Project. Her name was given by the “Adopt a Turtle” initiative and Littlewood Elementary School.


Kegan Magnolia was first tagged in 2017 on Wassaw NWR. She visited again to nest in 2019, 2021, and 2025. Previously, in 2011 and 2014, she nested on Hilton Head Island, Daufuskie Island, St. Catherine’s Island, and Little Tybee. She lays an average of 7 nests each year, with a total of 22 nests on Wassaw NWR, and 10 on other islands, for a grand total of 3,753 eggs, and 2,258 hatchlings that emerged.  At least 6 documented nests have been lost to storms or tidal surge.  Through the genetics project run by Dr. Brain Shamblin at UGA, we have determined that Kegan does not have any known relatives in the North Atlantic Recovery Unit at this time.

2832241.name: Niabi
2832241.description: The Niabi Zoo at Coal Valley, Illinois, is the main partner with Ch’ooj Ajauil AC. The name ‘Niabi’ reflects the meaning of "the fawn spared by the hunter" in the Native American Osage (Wazhazhe) language. This whale shark was previously tagged by Ch’ooj Ajauil (Rafael de la Parra) on July 7th 2009. When re-sighted on July 4th 2022, the tag was gone. ‘Bayonet’ was the original name because of the conspicuous shape of this shark's tail. This whale shark was designated as MXA-227 in the whale shark library (https://www.sharkbook.ai/) where photos of the skin patterning behind the gills of each shark are used to identify individual animals. Users can follow all of this shark’s encounters (more than 40) since 2009.

2881663.name: Brookes
2881663.description:
Meet white shark Brookes! This newly tagged white shark carries a name with deep meaning and community spirit on Big Tancook Island in Nova Scotia, Canada. The naming rights were won by Kathy Brookes-Weber at the Big Tancook Island fundraising summer carnival in August, an event that raised more than $14,000 to support the volunteer Big Tancook Emergency Response Association, the island’s Recreation Center, and the Chester Food Bank.


Kathy chose the name Brookes, her own last name, as a reminder that names hold power, presence, and stories. To her, sharks symbolize strength, resilience, and constant forward motion—they never stop moving, and neither should we when pursuing our goals or overcoming challenges.


By giving this shark her name, Kathy has tied her identity to these same qualities. Brookes is more than just a shark in the ocean—she’s a living emblem of courage, persistence, and the reminder that no matter how deep the waters get, we are built to keep swimming and moving forward with purpose.

2883372.name: Webster
2883372.description:
At over 12 feet long and 1,000 pounds strong, Webster is ready to tell us more about the secret lives of white sharks.


Webster is a powerful adult male white shark who now carries a story as vast as the ocean itself. At the time of tagging, he measured 12 ft. 2 in. and weighed an impressive 1,008.1 lbs.


Tagged in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, near the Tancook Islands, Webster joins OCEARCH’s ongoing Western North Atlantic study. By following his movements, our scientists are uncovering new insights into the behavior and migrations of this iconic species.


His name honors David Webster, a World War II soldier, shark enthusiast, and author of Myth and Maneater: The Story of the Shark. David Webster devoted his life to understanding and sharing the true nature of sharks. Tragically, he lost his life at sea, leaving behind a legacy of passion and respect. Naming this shark after him is a tribute to his courage and contribution to shark science.


This work was made possible through the support of the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams.


We invite you to follow Webster’s journey in real time on the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker™ as he navigates the wild expanse of the Atlantic.


#OCEARCH #SharkTracker #WhiteShark #SharkResearch #MarineScience #OceanConservation #WWII #DavidWebster

2884021.name: Ripple
2884021.description:
Ripple is an 11 ft. 6 in., 778 lb. sub-adult male white shark tagged on September 30, 2025, in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia. He represents the 106th white shark sampled in the Western North Atlantic (WNA) population, helping expand our understanding of this critical species. Ripple was tagged as part of our ongoing collaboration with the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station, where OCEARCH and our partners are working to better understand the summer and fall residency of white sharks in Atlantic Canada. This research is vital in piecing together the larger migration and life history puzzle of this keystone marine predator.


The name Ripple carries a powerful meaning. A ripple is the earliest sign of a wave—seemingly small, light, and playful on the surface, yet capable of growing into a force that moves oceans. In the same way, this sub-adult shark is just beginning his journey. Though young now, Ripple has the potential to grow into one of the giants of the sea, shaping the ecosystem around him as he matures.


Ripple is more than just a shark; he’s a living reminder of the power of beginnings. Like ripples on the water, even the smallest actions—whether in science, conservation, or our own lives—can build into something much greater. His presence in the Tracker invites us to follow along as his story unfolds, offering not only critical data for researchers but also inspiration for all of us to keep moving forward, no matter how small the first step may seem.

2885826.name: Goodall
2885826.description:
Meet Goodall, a newly tagged white shark on September 30th, 2025, she was tagged and released in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, by the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station Team, in collaboration with the OCEARCH Science and Fishing Teams. Goodall is a 13 ft. 1 in. adult female white shark named in honor of Dr. Jane Goodall, one of the world’s most influential pioneers in wildlife conservation. Dr. Goodall set a global standard for scientific investigation, dedicating her life to understanding animal behavior in the wild and inspiring generations of researchers and conservationists.


Like her namesake, Goodall the shark will play an important role in advancing science. As part of our collaborative research in Atlantic Canada, she will help provide up to ten years of data on the movement and behavior of white sharks in this critical region.


Goodall carries forward a legacy of curiosity, resilience, and dedication to protecting the natural world—an enduring symbol of the power of science to inspire change.


.

2885995.name: Nori
2885995.description:
Nori: The Playful Spirit of the North Atlantic


Bright, curious, and full of life, Nori is a young white shark exploring the cold, rich waters of the North Atlantic. This juvenile female, measuring 8 ft. 10 in. and weighing 423 lbs., was tagged on October 4, 2025, in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, as part of the Western North Atlantic white shark population (#110 WNA).


Her name, Nori—meaning “seaweed” in Japanese—celebrates the beauty and strength of ocean life. Seaweed may appear delicate, but it forms the foundation of thriving marine ecosystems, just as young sharks like Nori play an essential role in sustaining balance within the ocean.


Nori was tagged as part of our ongoing collaboration with the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station, where OCEARCH and our partners are studying the summer and fall residency of white sharks in Atlantic Canada. This research helps piece together the larger migration and life history puzzle of this important marine predator.


Follow Nori’s journey in real time on the OCEARCH Global Shark Tracker™ as she begins her adventure through the North Atlantic.


#OCEARCH #SharkTracker #WhiteShark #SharkResearch #MarineScience #OceanConservation #NovaScotia #Nori #AtlanticCanada

2886160.name: Brass Bed
2886160.description:
Brass Bed: A White Shark Born from Maritime Tradition


Brass Bed is a 9 ft. 2 in. (278 cm) female white shark tagged off the coast of Nova Scotia during OCEARCH’s ongoing field research in the Western North Atlantic population. This work helps scientists better understand the movement, health, and behavior of white sharks across this region—a key piece of the life-history puzzle that informs conservation worldwide.


Her name, Brass Bed, is rooted in a cherished piece of maritime lore. Years ago, a woman dreamed of owning a brass bed but was instead gifted a handcrafted boat named Brass Bed—a vessel that became a beloved part of her family’s life on the water. Inspired by that story, this shark’s name pays homage to the special bond between a boat and its name—a connection every mariner understands as a symbol of identity, pride, and enduring respect for the sea.


Like the sturdy vessel that once bore her name, Brass Bed represents strength, endurance, and grace in the waves—a living reflection of the maritime spirit that ties together those who work, explore, and find meaning on the ocean.

2886164.name: Ernst
2886164.description:
Ernst: The Connected White Shark of the North Atlantic


Ernst is a 12 ft. (365 cm) female white shark tagged off the coast of Nova Scotia during OCEARCH’s ongoing collaborative field research with the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station. This work helps scientists better understand the movement, health, and behavior of white sharks in Atlantic Canada—an essential step toward protecting these apex predators and the ecosystems they support.


The name Ernst was chosen by Team Tancook in honor of the ferry William G. Ernst, which has connected the communities of Big and Little Tancook Islands to the mainland since 1982. For more than four decades, this vessel has served as a lifeline for residents—providing vital transportation, fostering connection, and representing the strength of coastal communities.


Dedicated to the ferry’s hardworking crew, many of whom call Big Tancook Island home, Ernst the shark carries forward that same spirit of connection, resilience, and teamwork that keeps both island life and ocean research moving forward.

2886165.name: Cross
2886165.description:
White Shark Cross: Guiding the Way Through Atlantic Waters


Cross is a 9 ft. 1 in. (276 cm) juvenile male white shark tagged off the coast of Nova Scotia during OCEARCH’s ongoing field research to better understand how white sharks use Atlantic Canada’s coastal waters—whether passing through on migration or remaining to feed and grow.


Named after Cross Island in Lunenburg Bay, this shark’s name carries both natural and cultural significance. Folklore tells that early French settlers erected a cross on the island where the lighthouse now stands, serving as both a devotional symbol and a navigational aid for sailors. Today, the lighthouse continues to guide and protect mariners, just as the surrounding waters provide critical habitat for white sharks in the region.


The name Cross also honors one of the founding families of Big Tancook Island—recognizing their deep connection to the sea and their role in sustaining the island’s maritime heritage.


Through sharks like Cross, OCEARCH and our partners are shining a light on the vital ecosystems that support both people and predators across Atlantic Canada. This work is made possible through our collaboration with the Tancook Islands Marine Field Station, uniting science and community to protect our shared ocean.

Kab Xok ('shark world' in Mayan), is a cooperative formed by fishermen from Isla Mujeres dedicated to the monitoring and conservation of sharks and marine life through nature tourism and citizen science.


Saving Our Sharks is a non-profit organization dedicated to the conservation and research of sharks and marine life in the Mexican Caribbean for more than 13 years.


Ch’ooj Ajauil AC ('blue lordship' in Mayan), is a non-profit organization devoted to ensuring a healthy and sustainable future for the marine biodiversity of Mexican waters.
